title: Short Stuff: The Mars Rock with Signs of Life?
summary: Short Stuff episode on meteorite ALH84001, a rock found in Antarctica in December 1984 that was identified as a piece of Mars. The hosts cover its discovery by geologist Roberta Score, its journey from Mars, and the 1996 claim that it contained evidence of ancient microbial life. They describe the carbonate globes, the magnetite crystals and the PAH findings, the skeptic and believer camps, and the public announcement by President Clinton. They close by noting the debate is still unresolved and that the episode helped establish astrobiology.

segments.title: Introduction and naming of ALH84001
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and the Martian rock ALH84001, explaining how its name was derived from the Alan Hills region and its discovery as the first rock of the season. He notes geologist Roberta Score found it on a snowmobile.

segments.title: Origin of the Martian rock and its journey to Earth
segments.summary: The rock was stored for a long time before researchers realized it came from Mars. They describe it as about 4.5 billion years old, launched into space by a cataclysmic impact, drifting for about 16 million years, and landing in Antarctica after being captured by Earth's gravity.

segments.title: Carbonate grains and possible microbial traces
segments.summary: Orange carbonate grains inside the rock suggested water had once flowed on Mars. Researchers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory then noticed worm- and sausage-like structures near the carbonates that resembled Earth bacteria, but much smaller.

segments.title: Believers versus skeptics and the magnetite and PAH evidence
segments.summary: Believers and skeptics debated whether Earth contamination explained the findings. A microscopy specialist found magnetite crystals, which can be made by certain bacteria, and PAHs were also found, which can be byproducts of life though they can also form non-biologically.

segments.title: 1996 announcement and public reaction
segments.summary: The findings were submitted to Science and reviewed by a panel including Carl Sagan. NASA then announced the possibility of past life on Mars, with President Clinton making the announcement. Coverage was huge, and the hosts say it exceeded coverage of the first moon landing, though the scientific community was less receptive.

segments.title: Current status and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts say the debate is unresolved, that the rock helped found astrobiology, and they close the episode with a joke about the Ark of the Covenant.
